references.text: Luke previously tells us that Jesus had a habit of spending the nights on the Mount of Olives: "During the day he was in the temple teaching, but at night he went out and stayed on the mountain called the Mount of Olives" ([ref:Luk 21:37|Luke 21:37]). This confirms the expression "κατὰ τὸ ἔθος" (according to custom) in 22:39.

Matthew's parallel account states that Jesus went with his disciples to Gethsemane after the Last Supper: "Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane" ([ref:Matt 26:36|Matthew 26:36]). This is the same event seen from another gospel writer's perspective.

Mark's parallel account: "Then they came to a place called Gethsemane" ([ref:Mark 14:32|Mark 14:32]). Gethsemane was located at the foot of the Mount of Olives, confirming the location given in Luke's account.

John tells us that Jesus crossed the Kidron Valley to a garden, and that "Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples" ([ref:Joh 18:1-2|John 18:1-2]). This confirms that the Mount of Olives/garden was a place Jesus regularly visited.

Just before this, Jesus said to his disciples: "You are those who have stood by me in my trials" ([ref:Luk 22:28|Luke 22:28]). The fact that the disciples followed him (ἠκολούθησαν) to the Mount of Olives shows their loyalty, even though they would soon betray him.

The expression "κατὰ τὸ ἔθος" (according to custom/habit) is also used about Jesus in [ref:Luk 4:16|Luke 4:16], where he "as was his custom" went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day. Luke uses this expression to show Jesus' regular practice of devotion.

Zechariah prophesies about the Mount of Olives in the end times: "On that day his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, which lies east of Jerusalem" ([ref:Sak 14:4|Zechariah 14:4]). The Mount of Olives has messianic and eschatological significance in the OT, and Jesus' repeated presence there gives it deeper theological resonance.

David fled over the Mount of Olives when Absalom rebelled: "David went up weeping as he climbed the slope of the Mount of Olives" ([ref:2 Sam 15:30|2 Samuel 15:30]). The parallel between David, the suffering king on the Mount of Olives, and Jesus, the suffering Messiah in the same place, is an important typological connection.
